planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed in fall into lean, sandy, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun so it can cold-stratify naturally over winter; New England blazing star is a regional sand-plain endemic that resents rich, moisture-retentive garden loam.

directions: Direct sow fresh seed in fall into lean, sandy, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun, since this species is adapted to the open pine-oak sand plains and barrens of the northeastern coastal states rather than rich garden ground. It grows from a small corm and produces a loosely spaced, open arrangement of rounded, fuzzy purple flower heads along the upper stem in late summer, a looser and less formal look than the dense bottlebrush spikes of the common Liatris spicata. Because it is a rare, disturbance-dependent species that is state-listed as threatened or endangered across much of its range, seed or plants should come only from cultivated, nursery-propagated stock. Once established in sharply drained soil it needs no supplemental watering or fertilizer and resents being crowded by taller, more vigorous perennials.

common_name: Scrub Blazing Star (Lake Wales Ridge Blazing Star)

planting.note: Sow or plant nursery-propagated stock into deep, infertile, excessively drained white sand in full sun; this federally endangered species is restricted in the wild to the Lake Wales Ridge scrub of central Florida and needs the same sharp drainage in cultivation.

directions: Plant into deep, infertile, excessively drained white sand in full sun, replicating the ancient scrub ridges of central Florida's Polk and Highlands counties that are this species' only wild home. It grows from a corm and produces just a few flower heads per stem, but each head is unusually large and showy for the genus, opening into rich lavender-purple blooms more than an inch across in late summer and fall. Because it is federally listed as endangered and confined to a handful of imperiled scrub remnants, only nursery-propagated material from cultivated stock should ever be planted, never wild-collected divisions. It tolerates Florida's heat and drought extremely well but will rot quickly in any soil that holds moisture, so raised, unamended sandy beds are essential.

planting.note: Sow or plant into deep, infertile, well-drained coastal sand in full sun; Godfrey's blazing star is a narrow Florida Panhandle endemic restricted to the scrub and sandhills of Wakulla and Franklin counties.

directions: Plant into deep, infertile, excessively drained coastal sand in full sun, mimicking the scrub and sandhill dunes of the Florida Panhandle that make up this plant's entire known range. It grows from a corm and holds its small, stalkless, three- to four-flowered purple heads tight against the upper stem at a right angle, giving it a stiffer, more architectural look than the loose spikes of common gayfeather. Blooming from August into October, it provides late-season nectar for coastal pollinators in a habitat where flowering resources become scarce by late summer. It is state-listed as endangered due to its extremely limited range, so only nursery-grown, cultivated-stock plants should be used in gardens, sited where excellent drainage and full coastal sun can be guaranteed year-round.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into well-drained, sandy, infertile soil in full sun; graceful blazing star is native to the pine flatwoods, scrub, and sandhills of Florida, Georgia, and Alabama and is distinct from the similarly named Liatris tenuifolia.

directions: Direct sow in fall into well-drained, sandy, infertile soil in full sun, replicating the pine flatwoods, sandhills, and scrub habitats of the southeastern coastal plain where this species naturally occurs. Fine, soft hairs cover the wiry stems, and each flower head is held slightly away from the stem on a short stalk rather than pressed tight against it, giving the late-season purple flower spikes an airier, more open texture than many of its relatives. It flowers from late summer into fall and is a strong draw for bumblebees, long-tongued native bees, and migrating butterflies at a time when few other prairie perennials are still blooming. Established plants are very drought-tolerant thanks to a corm-like root system and need no fertilizer or irrigation once settled into lean, sharply drained sandy soil.

common_name: September Glory Liatris (Large-Flowered Eastern Blazing Star Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant corms or container plants in dry to well-drained, average soil in full sun in spring; September Glory is a selection of Liatris scariosa bred for extra-large flower heads and strong, straight stems well suited to cutting.

directions: Plant corms or container plants in dry to well-drained, average garden soil in full sun in spring, giving each clump room to form an upright, narrow column rather than crowding it among taller neighbors. September Glory carries fragrant, deep purple, button-like flower heads that are noticeably larger than those of typical blazing star cultivars, opening from the top of the tall spike downward as is characteristic of the genus and continuing to open new buds for weeks, which gives cut stems an exceptionally long vase life. Among the latest liatris selections to flower, it extends the blazing-star nectar season well into September, drawing bumblebees, skippers, and migrating monarchs when many other perennials have already faded. It is a genuinely low-water, low-maintenance plant once established, needing only a late-winter cutback and occasional division every several years to stay vigorous.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into shallow, rocky, sharply drained soil in full sun; Ouachita blazing star is a compact, short-statured species endemic to sandstone ridges and bluffs of the Ouachita Mountains in Arkansas and eastern Oklahoma.

directions: Direct sow in fall into shallow, rocky or weathered-sandstone soil with sharp drainage in full sun, matching the exposed ridges, bluffs, and open woods of the Ouachita Mountains that this regional endemic calls home. Once treated as a dwarf variety of Liatris squarrosa, it is now recognized as a distinct, shorter-growing species with tightly clustered flower heads wrapped in large, leaf-like bracts, giving each cluster a shaggier, more bracted look than its wider-ranging relative. It flowers earlier than most blazing stars, opening purple blooms as soon as May or June and continuing into September, which extends the nectar season for early-summer pollinators. Because its native range is small and specialized, it is best grown in a lean rock garden or gravel bed that stays dry, where it requires no fertilizer and very little care once established.

common_name: Blue Bird Liatris (Tall Blue-Purple Gayfeather Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant corms 2 to 3 inches deep in moist, well-drained soil in full sun around the last frost date; Blue Bird is a long-grown, tall-spiked blue-purple gayfeather cultivar distinct from the shorter Kobold and from the Floristan series.

directions: Plant corms 2 to 3 inches deep in moist, well-drained soil in full sun in mid-spring once hard frost danger has passed. Blue Bird produces tall, densely packed spikes of vivid blue-purple flowers on strong upright stems that reach well above the grassy summer foliage, opening from the top of the spike downward like all Liatris spicata selections. Its height and vase-friendly straight stems have long made it a favorite for the back of the perennial border as well as for cut-flower arrangements, where the fuzzy spikes hold their color for a week or more indoors. It is a strong pollinator plant, drawing bees and butterflies through its mid- to late-summer bloom period, and goldfinches will feed on the ripened seed if spent spikes are left standing into fall. Divide congested clumps of corms every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous flowering.
